questions.q: A decision tree scores 1.0 on training data but 0.63 on test data. What does this most likely indicate?
options: High bias, the model is too simple
The test set is too small to matter
High variance, the model is memorizing noise
The labels are perfectly predictable
questions.explain: A large gap between training and test performance is the classic sign of overfitting, or high variance.

questions.q: Which statement about a p-value is correct?
options: It is the probability that the null hypothesis is true
It is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null is true
It measures the size of the effect
A small p-value proves the effect is valuable
questions.explain: A p-value assumes the null is true; it does not give the chance the null is true or the effect's importance.

questions.q: Selecting features on the full dataset before cross-validation is a problem because:
options: It leaks information from the validation folds and inflates the score
It makes the model train more slowly
It removes too many rows
It only affects regression models
questions.explain: The selection step saw the labels of validation rows, so scores look better than they truly are; use a pipeline.

questions.q: With a 2% cancellation rate, a model that predicts 'no cancel' for everyone has what accuracy, and what does it teach?
options: 2%, so accuracy is stable
50%, since there are two classes
0%, since it catches no cancellations
98%, so accuracy alone is misleading for imbalanced data
questions.explain: Predicting the majority class gives 98% accuracy while catching no cancellers, so use precision, recall and PR-AUC.

questions.q: Why does peeking at an A/B test and stopping at the first significant result cause trouble?
options: It makes the sample size too large
It inflates the false-positive rate well above the nominal 5%
It removes the need for a control group
It lowers the effect size
questions.explain: Repeated looks give repeated chances for a false positive, so fix the sample size and duration in advance.
